clinicalPearls: Giardia (G. duodenalis, assemblages A and B in humans) is a non-invasive parasite confined to the proximal small bowel that does not spread hematogenously; an inoculum of as few as ~10 cysts can establish infection, and cysts resist routine chlorination but are killed by boiling or filtration.

Giardiasis classically presents with upper-intestinal/small-bowel features (nausea, vomiting, bloating, belching, sulfurous flatus, abdominal pain) and non-bloody diarrhea; fever, blood, or mucus in stool point away from giardiasis toward colitis or a concomitant illness.

Cryptosporidium (C. hominis, C. parvum) is self-limited (about 1-2 weeks) in immunocompetent hosts but causes chronic, profuse watery diarrhea with stool volumes ranging from 1 to 25 L/day in AIDS patients with CD4 counts below 100/uL.

Cystoisospora belli is distinctive among enteric protozoa in that it can produce peripheral eosinophilia in immunocompetent hosts; in AIDS it mimics cryptosporidiosis with chronic profuse watery diarrhea.

Cyclospora cayetanensis is linked to foodborne outbreaks from imported produce (basil, sweet peas, raspberries) and waterborne spread, and characteristically causes prolonged diarrhea that may persist beyond one month; absence of fecal blood and leukocytes indicates the small-bowel mucosa is not destroyed.

Conventional ova-and-parasite (O+P) stool examination does NOT reliably detect Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, or microsporidia; specific tests (modified acid-fast stain, immunoassays, direct fluorescent antibody, or NAATs) must be requested explicitly.

Microsporidia are obligate intracellular spore-forming organisms that are small and gram-positive; they are most often opportunistic in AIDS, where Enterocytozoon bieneusi and Encephalitozoon intestinalis cause chronic diarrhea and wasting and have been found in 10-40% of patients with chronic diarrhea.

Encephalitozoon species can disseminate beyond the gut to cause keratoconjunctivitis, sinusitis, bronchiolitis/respiratory disease, cholangitis, nephritis, and cystitis, so microsporidiosis is not solely an intestinal disease.

Balantidium coli is a large ciliated protozoan producing a large-bowel disease resembling amebiasis (mucosal invasion, focal necrosis, ulceration); it is zoonotic from pigs and, unlike amebiasis, only rarely disseminates hematogenously to other organs.
Blastocystis hominis has uncertain pathogenicity; finding it in stool warrants a full search for other bacterial, viral, or protozoal causes of diarrhea before attributing symptoms to it.

Dientamoeba fragilis is unique among intestinal protozoa in having only a trophozoite stage and no cyst stage; immediate fixation of stool improves detection of the labile trophozoites and NAATs outperform microscopy.

Trichomonas vaginalis is one of the most prevalent protozoal parasites in the United States (an estimated 2-3 million infections per year); it is essentially always transmitted venereally, and most infected men are asymptomatic, serving as a reservoir for reinfection.
harrison.pathophysiology: Most of these protozoa are acquired by fecal-oral ingestion of environmentally resistant cysts or oocysts (Trichomonas is the exception, being venereally transmitted). Giardia trophozoites excyst in the small intestine, adhere to but do not invade the proximal small-bowel epithelium, and may cause enterocyte apoptosis, epithelial barrier dysfunction, and malabsorption/secretion; the precise mechanism of diarrhea is unknown, and consequent loss of brush-border enzyme activity produces lactose intolerance and, in some chronic cases, malabsorption with villous flattening resembling tropical sprue or celiac disease. Cryptosporidium sporozoites infect intestinal epithelial cells within an intracellular vacuole, completing asexual and sexual cycles to generate immediately infectious oocysts; the means of secretory diarrhea are uncertain, infection can be patchy in the small bowel, and biliary tract involvement may cause papillary stenosis, sclerosing cholangitis, or cholecystitis, especially in AIDS. Cystoisospora and Cyclospora similarly invade small-bowel epithelial cells (Cyclospora oocysts must mature in the environment before becoming infectious). Microsporidia inject sporoplasm into host cells via an extruded polar tubule and replicate by merogony and sporogony, releasing spores in stool, urine, respiratory secretions, or other fluids. Hypogammaglobulinemia predisposes to prolonged, severe, treatment-refractory giardiasis, indicating humoral immunity is important for control.
additionalDifferentials: Tropical sprue (chronic giardiasis with villous flattening can resemble it)
Gluten-sensitive enteropathy / celiac disease (mimicked by chronic malabsorptive giardiasis)
Cystic fibrosis with superimposed enteric infection
Bacterial enteric infection (more acute, disabling course than giardiasis)
Lactose intolerance (may follow giardiasis from brush-border enzyme loss)
infectionMimics: Amebiasis (Entamoeba histolytica) versus balantidiasis in the colon
Other infectious vaginitis (bacterial vaginosis, vulvovaginal candidiasis) versus trichomonal vaginitis - clinical features do not reliably distinguish them
Cryptosporidiosis, cystoisosporiasis, cyclosporiasis, and microsporidiosis can clinically overlap as causes of chronic watery diarrhea in AIDS
Other bacterial, viral, or protozoal diarrhea when Blastocystis hominis is detected
nonInfectiousMimics: Inflammatory bowel disease (for invasive colonic balantidiasis)
additionalInvestigations: Stool ova-and-parasite examination (detects Giardia and Balantidium but is insufficient for Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, microsporidia)
Fecal modified acid-fast staining (Cryptosporidium, Cystoisospora, Cyclospora oocysts)
Direct immunofluorescent antibody (Giardia, Cryptosporidium; and for Trichomonas, more sensitive at 70-90% than wet mount)
Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) - highly sensitive across the protozoa and useful for microsporidial speciation
Modified trichrome or fluorescent stains of stool/urine/tissue for microsporidia; electron microscopy often required in tissue
Repeated stool sampling, duodenal fluid aspiration, and small-bowel biopsy when cyst/oocyst excretion is intermittent or low-level
Wet-mount microscopy of vaginal or prostatic secretions for motile trichomonads (sensitivity only ~50-60%); NAATs on urine or vaginal/endocervical swabs are first-line
redFlags: CD4+ T-cell count below 100/uL with watery diarrhea (risk of severe, chronic, profuse cryptosporidiosis)
Very high stool output (up to 25 L/day) with marked fluid and electrolyte depletion in immunocompromised cryptosporidiosis
Significant weight loss, wasting, dehydration, or growth retardation in children with chronic giardiasis or cryptosporidiosis
Right-upper-quadrant or mid-epigastric pain suggesting biliary tract involvement (cryptosporidiosis or microsporidiosis: papillary stenosis, sclerosing cholangitis, cholecystitis)
Hypogammaglobulinemia presenting with prolonged, treatment-refractory giardiasis
Fever, blood, or mucus in stool during presumed giardiasis - suggests an alternative diagnosis or coinfection
Eosinophilia with enteric symptoms (suggests cystoisosporiasis among the enteric protozoa, or sarcocystosis-associated myositis)
Disseminated microsporidiosis (fever, sinusitis, cholangitis, bronchiolitis, keratoconjunctivitis, encephalitis) in AIDS
harrison.prognosis: Outcomes depend heavily on immune status. Giardiasis ranges from asymptomatic carriage to fulminant diarrhea and malabsorption; most patients are cured, though some with chronic infection have delayed symptom resolution attributed to slow brush-border enzyme regeneration, and hypogammaglobulinemic or AIDS patients may have refractory disease. Cryptosporidiosis is self-limited (1-2 weeks) in immunocompetent hosts but can be chronic and severe in AIDS, where improved immune status from antiretroviral therapy can lead to resolution. Cystoisosporiasis and cyclosporiasis can be self-limited but tend to relapse and become chronic in HIV-infected patients. Microsporidiosis can be self-limited in the immunocompetent but contributes to chronic diarrhea and wasting in AIDS, and definitive therapy is not well established. Balantidiasis ranges from asymptomatic to fulminant dysentery; sarcocystosis and most Blastocystis or Dientamoeba infections are mild or self-limited.
pitfalls: Relying on routine stool O+P examination, which misses Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, and microsporidia - specific stains or NAATs must be ordered
Stopping at a single stool exam: cyst/oocyst excretion is variable and intermittent, so repeated sampling or duodenal aspiration/biopsy may be needed
Attributing symptoms to Blastocystis hominis without excluding other pathogens, given its uncertain pathogenicity
Missing Dientamoeba fragilis because of delayed fixation of stool, which degrades its labile trophozoites (it has no cyst stage)
Assuming routine water chlorination eliminates Giardia and Cryptosporidium - their cysts/oocysts resist standard chlorination; boiling or submicron filtration is needed
Diagnosing trichomonal vaginitis by wet mount alone, given its modest (~50-60%) sensitivity
Treating trichomoniasis without concurrently treating sexual partners, leading to apparent treatment failure that is actually reinfection (true high-level metronidazole resistance also occurs)
harrison.severityClassification: No formal staging; severity is gauged clinically by host immune status (notably CD4 count below 100/uL marking risk of severe cryptosporidiosis), stool volume and degree of fluid/electrolyte loss (up to 25 L/day in severe cryptosporidiosis), presence of malabsorption/weight loss/wasting, dehydration, growth retardation in children, and biliary or disseminated extraintestinal involvement.
management: Pathogen-directed antimicrobials: a nitroimidazole (metronidazole or tinidazole) for giardiasis and trichomoniasis, nitazoxanide for cryptosporidiosis, co-trimoxazole for Cystoisospora and Cyclospora, and albendazole (with fumagillin for Enterocytozoon) for microsporidiosis
Rehydration and electrolyte correction with oral rehydration solution or intravenous fluids for profuse watery diarrhoea
In HIV-related cryptosporidiosis or microsporidiosis, prioritise immune restoration with antiretroviral therapy, which is central to clearance
For trichomoniasis, treat sexual partners concurrently and screen for coexisting sexually transmitted infections
Nutritional support and management of malabsorption and secondary lactose intolerance in protracted giardiasis
Public health measures with safe-water, hand-hygiene and food-handling advice, and reporting of foodborne or waterborne outbreaks
Consider combination or alternative regimens for refractory giardiasis and confirm cure or exclude persisting infection in immunocompromised hosts
